title: THEY CAN CAST OUT DEMONS… BUT CAN THEY CAST OUT THE HATRED IN THEIR OWN HEARTS?
paragraphs: THEY CAN CAST OUT DEMONS… BUT CAN THEY CAST OUT THE HATRED IN THEIR OWN HEARTS?

Why are some Christians fearless when confronting darkness in the spiritual realm, yet strangely silent when racism, greed, and injustice are standing right in front of them? Jesus warned us about a kind of religion that looks powerful in public while quietly resisting the very transformation He came to bring.
There is something deeply unsettling happening in parts of modern Christianity.
A person can spend three hours discussing demonic oppression, spiritual warfare, generational curses, and the schemes of Satan…
Yet become visibly uncomfortable when someone mentions racism.
They can passionately rebuke the spirit of poverty while refusing to question the greed that exploits the poor.
They can identify supposed demonic influences in music, movies, clothing, and culture, but struggle to recognize the cruelty in their own words.
They can pray against darkness in a city while remaining silent when the vulnerable are mistreated in that very same city.
And perhaps the most disturbing possibility is this:
Sometimes the darkness we are most eager to confront is the darkness that requires the least repentance from us personally.
Read that again.
Because this is not an attack on spiritual warfare.
The Bible is unmistakably clear that spiritual evil is real. Jesus confronted demons. The apostles encountered demonic opposition. Paul instructed believers to stand against the schemes of the devil.
But something has gone terribly wrong when Christians become more fascinated with identifying demons in other people than recognizing sin in themselves.
And before anyone starts thinking about that one pastor, that one denomination, that one political movement, or that one Christian who desperately needs to read this…
There is a question we need to answer first.
What if Jesus is speaking to us?
What if the problem is not merely what the Church refuses to confront?
What if the problem is what we have learned to excuse?
Because a person can know the vocabulary of spiritual warfare and still be spiritually immature.
A person can speak passionately about holiness and still harbor prejudice.
A person can preach against the devil and still worship money.
And a person can appear deeply religious while repeatedly walking past the very people Jesus commanded them to love.
That is not a new problem.
Jesus confronted it two thousand years ago.
And His words are still capable of shaking the foundations of our comfortable Christianity.
In Matthew 23:23, Jesus confronted religious leaders who were meticulous about giving a tenth of even their herbs while neglecting what He called the weightier matters of the law.
Justice.
Mercy.
Faithfulness.
The Greek text uses the expression τὰ βαρύτερα τοῦ νόμου (ta barytera tou nomou).
Literally, the weightier matters of the law.
Jesus was not telling them to abandon obedience in smaller things. He explicitly said they should practice the weightier matters without neglecting the others.
His accusation was far more devastating.
They were carefully practicing visible religious duties while neglecting the moral responsibilities that revealed the condition of their hearts.
Imagine standing before Jesus with a record of religious activity.
You attended worship.
You fasted.
You prayed.
You gave offerings.
You defended biblical doctrine.
You argued passionately against spiritual darkness.
And then Jesus asks about the people you mistreated.
The worker whose wages you withheld.
The stranger you despised because of their ethnicity.
The poor family whose suffering you dismissed.
The person you humiliated because they looked different, spoke differently, or came from another social class.
The neighbor whose pain you refused to acknowledge because doing so would have made your life uncomfortable.
Suddenly, religious activity no longer feels like a hiding place.
Because Jesus is not impressed by the appearance of holiness when the heart remains unwilling to love.
And here is where this becomes painfully personal.
Sometimes it is easier to pray against an invisible enemy than apologize to someone we have visibly wounded.
It is easier to shout, "I rebuke you, Satan!" than whisper, "I was wrong. Please forgive me."
It is easier to discuss demonic strongholds than admit that prejudice has become a stronghold in our own thinking.
It is easier to condemn the greed of billionaires than examine our own dishonesty, selfish ambition, or unwillingness to share.
It is easier to demand justice for people we agree with than extend fairness to people we dislike.
And it is easier to call ourselves defenders of truth than allow the truth to defend someone we would rather ignore.

Not every Christian who discusses demons is avoiding justice. Many believers faithfully pursue both spiritual discernment and practical righteousness. Nor is every disagreement about a social issue evidence of racism or hatred.
But whenever our religious convictions consistently protect us from examining our own sin, we should be concerned.
Because biblical discernment does not merely identify what is wrong with the world.
It allows God's Word to expose what is wrong within us.
Hebrews 4:12 describes the Word of God as living and active, able to discern the thoughts and intentions of the heart.
Not just somebody else's heart.
Ours.
And sometimes the most frightening thing about opening Scripture is discovering that the passage we wanted to use against someone else was meant to confront us first.
Consider the story Jesus told in Luke 10.
A man was traveling from Jerusalem to Jericho when robbers attacked him, stripped him, beat him, and left him half dead.
A priest came down the road.
He saw the wounded man.
And passed by on the other side.
Then a Levite approached.
He also saw him.
And passed by.
These were men associated with religious life.
They were not strangers to sacred responsibilities.
Yet the wounded man remained abandoned.
Then came a Samaritan.
To appreciate the force of this story, we must remember that serious ethnic and religious tensions existed between Jews and Samaritans.
Jesus deliberately made the compassionate outsider the moral example.
The Samaritan approached the wounded man, treated his injuries, transported him to an inn, and paid for his care.
The story is not merely about having sympathetic feelings.
Compassion cost him something.
Time.
Money.
Convenience.
Personal involvement.
Jesus then asked which traveler had proved to be a neighbor to the wounded man.
The answer was the one who showed mercy.
And Jesus commanded, "Go, and do thou likewise" (Luke 10:37, KJV).
Now imagine the priest had stopped to pray against the demons responsible for the robbery.
Imagine the Levite had delivered a passionate sermon about the spiritual darkness affecting the road to Jericho.
Imagine both men had spoken with perfect theological vocabulary.
But neither had helped the bleeding man.
Would their words have changed the condition of the person lying in the dust?
Prayer matters.
Spiritual warfare matters.
But Jesus did not tell the lawyer in Luke 10 to admire the Samaritan's religious language.
He commanded him to imitate his mercy.
A wounded neighbor does not become less wounded because we have correctly identified the existence of evil.
And some of us need to hear that.
Because we have become skilled at explaining darkness while remaining reluctant to carry light into the places where people are suffering.
We speak about spiritual bondage but ignore human trafficking.
We condemn wickedness but remain indifferent to exploitation.
We denounce the devil's hatred while allowing ethnic hostility to remain unchallenged among us.
We preach generosity while quietly treating financial success as evidence of spiritual superiority.
And when someone raises these contradictions, we sometimes accuse them of being divisive.
But is it always division to expose injustice?
Or can it be an act of faithfulness?
The prophet Isaiah addressed a religious community that practiced fasting while simultaneously exploiting workers and engaging in conflict.
In Isaiah 58:6, God described the kind of fasting He desired as one that loosens the bonds of wickedness, releases oppressive burdens, and lets the oppressed go free.
The Hebrew text includes the expression פַּתֵּחַ חַרְצֻבּוֹת רֶשַׁע (patteakh chartsubbot resha).
It speaks of loosening the bonds or restraints of wickedness.
The passage continues by calling God's people to share bread with the hungry, provide shelter for the poor, and clothe the naked.
Notice what God was confronting.
Not the absence of religious activity.
The contradiction between religious activity and unrighteous conduct.
They were fasting.
But their treatment of others contradicted the purpose of their worship.
They were seeking God.
But refusing to practice the justice and mercy His character required.
And this is where the modern Church must be extraordinarily careful.
Because we can create impressive worship experiences while neglecting the suffering beyond our walls.
We can organize conferences about spiritual breakthrough while overlooking the people whose lives are being broken by exploitation.
We can raise our hands during worship while refusing to extend those same hands toward someone we have been taught to fear.
And we can become so preoccupied with what demons might be doing that we stop asking what the Holy Spirit is commanding us to do.
The Holy Spirit does not lead believers into indifference toward the image-bearers of God.
He produces love.
Galatians 5:22 identifies love as the first characteristic in the fruit of the Spirit.
Not spectacle.
Not popularity.
Not spiritual intimidation.
Love.
And biblical love is not sentimental approval of everything another person believes or does.
It is a Christ-shaped commitment to seek their good in truth, humility, and righteousness.
That includes people whose backgrounds are different from ours.
People whose politics we dislike.
People whose suffering challenges our assumptions.
People whose stories expose injustices we would rather believe do not exist.
And people who cannot offer us anything in return.
In Acts 17:26, Paul declares that God made the nations from one, emphasizing humanity's common origin under the Creator.
Genesis 1:27 teaches that human beings are created in God's image.
James 2 condemns favoritism within the Christian assembly, particularly the preference shown to the wealthy over the poor.
And Revelation 7:9 presents a vision of a redeemed multitude from every nation, tribe, people, and language standing before God's throne and the Lamb.
Think about that.
The eternal worship of Jesus Christ includes people from every nation.
Yet some Christians struggle to treat people of another ethnicity with dignity in the present.
How can we celebrate a multiethnic multitude in heaven while defending racial contempt on earth?
How can we rejoice that Christ has purchased people from every people group while behaving as though certain people are less worthy of respect?
How can we preach reconciliation with God while refusing to pursue reconciliation with the people we have wronged?
Racism is not merely an unfortunate personality flaw when it expresses contempt for people because of their ancestry or ethnicity.
It contradicts the biblical dignity of human beings made in God's image.
And when racial prejudice becomes embedded in institutions, practices, or systems, Christians should be willing to examine the evidence and seek what is just.
That does not require accepting every political slogan, theory, or proposed solution.
Christians may disagree about policies and the causes of particular inequalities.
But we cannot use those disagreements as permission to abandon truthfulness, impartiality, compassion, or justice.
Our loyalty to Jesus must be greater than our loyalty to any tribe, party, culture, or ideology.
And sometimes faithfulness means admitting that people on our own side have done wrong.
That kind of honesty is uncomfortable.
But repentance was never meant to be a comfortable performance.
The Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia), commonly translated "repentance," speaks of a change of mind or turning that, in biblical usage, is inseparable from a transformed response to God.
Repentance is not simply feeling embarrassed after being exposed.
It is turning from sin toward God.
It is admitting what is wrong without dressing it in religious excuses.
It is making restitution when appropriate and possible.
It is learning to love where we once despised.
It is surrendering the pride that keeps insisting we have nothing to confess.
And perhaps that is why confronting racism, greed, and injustice can feel more threatening than discussing demons.
Because it may require us to change.
It may cost us approval.
It may expose our hypocrisy.
It may challenge our financial habits.
It may force us to confront the ways we have benefited from unfairness or contributed to someone else's suffering.
It may require a difficult conversation with a family member.
It may mean refusing to laugh at a racist joke.
It may mean paying workers fairly when underpaying them would be more profitable.
It may mean listening to someone's experience before dismissing it.
It may mean admitting that our favorite preacher, political leader, or Christian organization was wrong.
And none of those things can be accomplished merely by shouting at the devil.
They require humility before God.
They require obedience.
They require the kind of discipleship that follows Jesus even when following Him costs us something.
But we must also confront another temptation.
The temptation to turn justice itself into a substitute for the Gospel.
Because activism cannot save us.
Moral outrage cannot forgive our sins.
Political reform, however necessary or beneficial, cannot regenerate the human heart.
Only Jesus Christ can reconcile sinners to God.
Only His death and resurrection provide the foundation of our salvation.
Only His grace can transform the deepest roots of human rebellion.
We must never reduce Christianity to social activism.
But neither should we reduce Christianity to religious language that leaves our treatment of others unchanged.
The Gospel is not less than forgiveness of sins.
And the forgiveness of sins produces a new life.
Ephesians 2:8–10 teaches that we are saved by grace through faith, not by works, and that we are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
The order matters.
We do not earn salvation by fighting injustice.
We pursue righteousness and mercy because God's grace has begun transforming us.
We do not love our neighbor to purchase God's acceptance.
We love because we have first been loved.
We do not repent to prove we are worthy of Jesus.
We repent because Jesus is worthy of our surrender.
And if we forget that order, we will eventually turn even good causes into opportunities for self-righteousness.
The answer to hypocrisy is not another kind of hypocrisy.
The answer is Christ.
Look at Zacchaeus.
Luke 19 tells us that he was a chief tax collector and a wealthy man.
Tax collection under Roman rule was associated with opportunities for financial exploitation, and Zacchaeus himself acknowledged the possibility of having defrauded others.
When Jesus entered his life, something remarkable happened.
Zacchaeus declared that he would give half his possessions to the poor and restore fourfold what he had wrongfully taken.
Jesus responded by declaring that salvation had come to his house.
Notice what changed.
His encounter with Jesus did not end with an emotional religious experience.
It reached his wallet.
His treatment of others.
His willingness to make wrongs right.
His relationship with wealth.
He did not merely announce that he had been spiritually delivered.
He demonstrated a changed direction through concrete acts of repentance.
And that should make every one of us uncomfortable in the healthiest possible way.
Because sometimes the most convincing evidence of spiritual transformation is not how loudly someone speaks about demons.
It is how differently they treat people after meeting Jesus.
The dishonest employer begins paying fairly.
The prejudiced believer begins confronting the hatred they once defended.
The greedy person becomes generous.
The proud person learns to apologize.
The indifferent Christian begins noticing the suffering they previously walked past.
The person who once used Scripture to justify contempt begins reading Scripture with humility and fear of God.
Not perfectly.
Not without struggle.
Not without failures that require fresh confession and repentance.
But genuinely.
Because grace does not merely offer us a new religious vocabulary.
Grace begins making us new.
And there is one passage that should silence every attempt to separate impressive spiritual activity from obedience to Christ.
Matthew 7:22–23.
Jesus warns that many will appeal to extraordinary religious works done in His name, including prophecy, casting out demons, and mighty works.
Yet He says that He will declare to some of them that He never knew them, calling them workers of lawlessness.
Consider the seriousness of that warning.
Jesus does not say that the ability to speak about demons proves someone belongs to Him.
He does not say that public spiritual activity automatically reveals a surrendered heart.
He warns against trusting religious achievements while living in disobedience.
This passage is not permission for us to pronounce judgment on the salvation of particular people.
It is a warning that should lead each of us to examine ourselves.
Because the most dangerous spiritual deception may not be believing that demons exist.
It may be believing that our religious performance makes repentance unnecessary.
And before we go any further, I want to speak to someone who has been wounded by this contradiction.
Perhaps you experienced racism from people who called themselves Christians.
Perhaps you were exploited by someone who quoted Scripture while withholding what they owed you.
Perhaps you watched a church defend a powerful person while ignoring those who had been harmed.
Perhaps you were told to remain silent because speaking about injustice would damage the reputation of a ministry.
Perhaps the people who should have protected you used religious language to dismiss your pain.
I cannot tell you that every person who claims to represent Jesus has represented Him faithfully.
Scripture itself warns us otherwise.
But I can tell you this:
The hypocrisy of those who misuse His name does not define the character of Christ.
Jesus did not overlook religious hypocrisy.
He exposed it.
Jesus did not praise those who devoured the vulnerable while performing impressive acts of devotion.
He condemned such behavior.
Jesus did not treat the wounded as disposable inconveniences.
He moved toward people who were suffering.
And at the cross, He did something none of us could do for ourselves.
He bore sin.
The sin of the proud.
The sin of the prejudiced.
The sin of the greedy.
The sin of the cruel.
The sin of the self-righteous.
And the sin of those who know exactly what righteousness requires but repeatedly refuse to practice it.
Isaiah 53:6 declares that all of us have gone astray and that the Lord laid upon His suffering servant the iniquity of us all.
The cross is not a place where we gather to congratulate ourselves for being morally superior to other sinners.
It is where our pride is exposed and our desperate need for mercy becomes undeniable.
The same Jesus who commands repentance offers forgiveness to those who turn to Him in faith.
The same Savior who confronts hypocrisy welcomes the repentant sinner.
The same Lord who demands love for our neighbors gives His Spirit to transform hearts that have been shaped by hatred.
And the resurrection declares that sin and death do not have the final word.
This is the scandal of grace.
Not that God pretends our sins do not matter.
But that the sinless Son of God gave Himself to rescue sinners who could never rescue themselves.
And those whom He rescues are called to follow Him into a new way of living.
From prejudice to love.
From greed to generosity.
From indifference to mercy.
From self-righteousness to repentance.
From religious performance to genuine surrender.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the past never happened.
But by bringing forgiveness, truth, accountability, reconciliation, and transformation into places we once believed were beyond redemption.
Now imagine what would happen if the Church took both spiritual warfare and biblical justice seriously.
Imagine believers praying fervently against evil while also refusing to participate in it.
Imagine pastors preaching repentance with the same conviction whether the sin involved sexual immorality, racism, greed, dishonesty, or oppression.
Imagine Christian employers treating their workers with dignity.
Imagine churches becoming places where the wealthy are not automatically honored above the poor.
Imagine people from different ethnic backgrounds worshiping together without being pressured to ignore genuine wounds.
Imagine Christians disagreeing about politics without abandoning their obligation to love one another.
Imagine a generation of believers who understood that fighting the good fight of faith includes resisting the devil and refusing to surrender their character to hatred.
Ephesians 6:12 reminds us that our struggle is not against flesh and blood.
That truth should make us more careful about how we treat human beings, not less.
People are not the ultimate enemy.
Our neighbors are not demons.
Someone from another race is not our enemy because of their ancestry.
A person who challenges our assumptions is not automatically an instrument of Satan.
And someone who has suffered injustice is not being unspiritual merely because they ask Christians to respond with integrity.
We can confront falsehood without dehumanizing people.
We can resist wickedness without becoming cruel.
We can uphold biblical convictions without abandoning biblical compassion.
And we can proclaim the power of Christ over darkness while recognizing that one of the places His light must shine is inside our own hearts.
So here is the question I want to leave with you.
Not whether you believe demons exist.
Not whether you know how to quote Ephesians 6.
Not whether you have ever attended a deliverance service.
But this:
What sin are you willing to confront in someone else that you are still unwilling to surrender in yourself?
Think about it.
Is it prejudice?
Is it greed?
Is it pride?
Is it indifference toward suffering?
Is it a habit of defending injustice when it benefits someone you admire?
Is it the need to appear righteous while secretly resisting the changes God is calling you to make?
You do not have to announce every private struggle to the world.
But you do need to bring it honestly before the Lord.
And perhaps your next act of spiritual warfare will not look dramatic at all.
Perhaps it will look like a sincere apology.
Perhaps it will look like returning money that was never yours.
Perhaps it will look like defending someone being mistreated.
Perhaps it will look like asking God to expose the prejudice you inherited but never questioned.
Perhaps it will look like choosing mercy when bitterness feels easier.
Perhaps it will look like opening your Bible, falling to your knees, and praying:

"Lord Jesus, I have spent so much time recognizing what is wrong with others that I have neglected what You are confronting in me. Forgive my pride. Expose my hypocrisy. Remove the hatred I have excused, the greed I have defended, and the indifference I have disguised as wisdom. Teach me to love what You love, hate what is evil, and walk humbly before You. I cannot transform my own heart. I need Your grace. Make me more like You. Amen."
Not as a performance.
Not because strangers need to know your private sins.
But as a simple expression of your willingness to be corrected and transformed by Jesus.
You do not owe anyone the details of your pain.
There may be someone reading those words who realizes they are not alone in their struggle.
There may be another believer who finally finds the courage to acknowledge a wrong.
There may be someone who has almost abandoned Christianity because of religious hypocrisy and begins to understand that Jesus Himself condemned the very behavior that wounded them.
Not to win an argument.
Not to shame people.
But because conversations about biblical justice, repentance, mercy, and the transforming power of Christ belong within the Church, not outside its concern.
Someone in your family may need to read this.
A friend may be quietly wrestling with prejudice they have never acknowledged.
A church leader may need a reminder that spiritual authority must never become an excuse for moral blindness.
A struggling believer may need to discover that Jesus is not calling them to pretend everything is fine.
And someone who does not yet believe may need to see that Christianity, faithfully understood, does not require defending hypocrisy.
Our desire is not to build an audience addicted to religious controversy.
It is to help build disciples whose lives increasingly reflect Jesus Christ.
Gospel-centered discipleship requires more than one powerful article.
It requires returning to Scripture when emotions fade, confronting difficult truths when conviction becomes uncomfortable, and receiving encouragement when the journey of obedience feels exhausting.

Through Gospel Warrior, we want to continue producing Christ-centered teaching, devotional encouragement, biblical reflections, and resources that point people toward repentance, forgiveness, spiritual maturity, and genuine transformation.
Scripture calls believers to give willingly, thoughtfully, and without compulsion. As 2 Corinthians 9:7 teaches, God loves a cheerful giver.
You are not less valuable to God.
You are not less welcome in this community.
Your prayers, your thoughtful comments, your willingness to share biblical truth, and your personal obedience to Jesus matter.
What matters most is that Christ is honored, Scripture is handled faithfully, and people are pointed toward Him rather than toward a personality, platform, or brand.
It is a growing community of people who love Jesus enough to let His Word change them.
And now, one final thought.
One day, every mask will fall.
Every carefully constructed religious reputation will lose its power to impress.
Every hidden motive will be known to the Lord who sees the heart.
On that day, our public image will not be able to replace a genuine relationship with Christ.
The question will not be how many arguments we won about demons.
Or how many people admired our spiritual vocabulary.
Or how convincingly we appeared righteous in front of others.
The question that should concern us now is whether we truly know Jesus and are responding to His grace with repentant faith.
Because the Savior who commands us to love our neighbors is the same Savior who died for our sins.
And the Lord who exposes our hypocrisy is the same Lord who welcomes sinners who turn to Him.
Do not run from His conviction.
Do not confuse His correction with rejection.
Do not protect the very sin He is calling you to surrender.
Come to Him.
Bring your pride.
Bring your prejudice.
Bring your greed.
Bring your indifference.
Bring the wounds inflicted by others.
Bring the shame of your own failures.
Come honestly, trusting not in your ability to make yourself righteous but in the crucified and risen Christ, who alone can save.
And then follow Him.
Not just into conversations about spiritual warfare.
But into the costly, beautiful obedience of loving God and loving your neighbor.
Because the darkness you keep rebuking in the world must never become the darkness you refuse to surrender in your own heart.
